Chapter 7. Family Ties: Healing Old Wounds and Rewriting the Past.
You know, family shapes us in ways we don’t always realize—sometimes for the better, sometimes not so much. The stories we grow up with, the little rules and silent expectations, even the disappointments—they all have a way of sticking around, long after we’ve moved on.
For a lot of us, that feeling of being "unwifeable" can actually trace its roots all the way back to childhood. Think about it—the things we picked up from our parents, our siblings, or just the world around us. Those messages, even the ones nobody ever said out loud, can really linger.
Trying to reconnect with family isn’t always simple, is it? Old wounds come bubbling up, and suddenly you find yourself slipping right back into those old roles. Maybe there’s a parent who never quite got you, who seemed to love you only if you lived up to their idea of who you should be. Or maybe there’s that sibling who always looked like they had it all figured out—a constant reminder of what you’re not. Even holidays or simple phone calls can feel like you’re stepping into a minefield, where misunderstanding and hurt are always just one word away.
But as you start to do the work—really look at your own healing—something changes. You want to heal those old wounds, even if it’s hard. And it usually starts small. Maybe it’s just a phone call, or a letter. Maybe it’s a conversation that’s a little more honest than you ever managed before. Sure, there’s fear. Maybe some anger too. But there’s also this growing sense of compassion—not just for yourself, but for the people who raised you. Suddenly, you see that everyone’s carrying their own pain, their own regrets, their own quiet hope to be understood and loved.
Picture this: one afternoon, you’re sitting across from a parent at the old kitchen table. The past comes up. There are tears, maybe even apologies. Stories get shared that you never thought you’d say out loud. And no, it’s not some magical fix—those patterns don’t just vanish overnight. But you can feel something shift. That desperate need for approval starts to fade, replaced by this quiet acceptance. You realize, maybe for the first time, that you can love your family without letting their expectations define your life.
Forgiveness, it turns out, isn’t really about saying what happened was okay. It’s about freeing yourself from the past’s grip—letting go of the wish that things could’ve been different, and turning your attention to what’s actually possible now. It’s a process, and there are ups and downs, setbacks and little breakthroughs. But with every honest conversation, every moment of truth, those old family stories start to lose their hold just a little bit.
Family will probably always be complicated. But instead of feeling trapped, you start to see it as part of your bigger story—a mix of pain and strength, a reminder of where you came from and just how far you’ve made it.
